name: Accountant
summary: Accountant interviews usually check your fundamentals (journal entries, reconciliations, the month-end close and the basics of tax) and how careful you are with detail. Candidates commonly report questions on the software they've used and, for some roles, a practical test in Excel or an accounting package; audit and tax roles add questions on standards, compliance and working with clients.
rounds: Technical interview on accounting basics, reconciliations, month-end close and tax
Practical test in Excel or accounting software (for some roles)
Interview with the finance, audit or tax manager on past work and judgement
looks_for: Sound basics: double entry, accruals, depreciation, reconciliations
Attention to detail and checking your own work
Knowing the compliance deadlines and rules the role involves
Comfort with Excel and accounting software
Integrity: raising problems rather than hiding them
Explaining numbers clearly to people outside accounts

questions.text: Tell me about a time you found an error in the accounts. How did you trace it?
covers: How you noticed something was wrong
The steps you took to trace it to the source
How you corrected it and what you put in place so it didn't recur

questions.text: Tell me about a month-end or year-end close you worked on. What was your part, and what went wrong?
covers: Your tasks and the deadline
One problem that came up and how you solved it
What you'd do earlier next time

questions.text: Describe a time you were asked to record something in a way you weren't comfortable with.
covers: What you were asked to do and why it concerned you
How you raised it, with the rule or evidence behind your concern
What happened, and what you'd do if pushed again

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to get documents or answers from a difficult client or colleague on time.
covers: What you needed and why it was late
How you followed up and made it easy for them to respond
The outcome and how you kept the relationship good

questions.text: Explain accrual accounting, and give me an example of an accrued expense.
covers: Recording income and expenses in the period they belong to, not when cash moves
An example such as electricity used this month but billed next month
The journal entry, and reversing it when the bill arrives

questions.text: Walk me through a bank reconciliation. What causes the differences, and how do you clear them?
covers: Matching the bank statement against the cash book
Timing items like uncleared cheques and deposits in transit, plus bank charges and errors
Investigating old unmatched items rather than carrying them forward

questions.text: What's the difference between a provision and a reserve?
covers: A provision is charged against profit for a known liability or loss of uncertain amount, such as warranties
A reserve is profit set aside within equity, such as a general reserve
Provisions reduce profit; reserves are set aside out of profit

questions.text: How would you tell capital expenditure from revenue expenditure? Give me an example of each.
covers: Capital spending creates or improves an asset that lasts beyond the year
Revenue spending keeps the business running day to day
An example pair, such as buying a machine versus repairing it

questions.text: The trial balance doesn't tally. What would you check, and in what order?
covers: Totals and balances carried forward correctly
Entries posted to one side only, wrong amounts or swapped digits
The suspense account, and the largest or most recent entries first

questions.text: In simple terms, how does input tax credit work under GST or VAT?
covers: Tax paid on purchases can be set against tax collected on sales
Conditions such as a valid invoice and the supplier reporting the sale correctly
Why mismatches between your books and the tax returns matter

questions.text: Explain tax deducted at source, or withholding tax, and what the accounts team has to do about it.
covers: Deducting tax when paying certain bills or salaries
Depositing it and filing returns on time
Issuing certificates and reconciling with the tax records

questions.text: How would you speed up the month-end close without losing accuracy?
covers: A checklist with owners and deadlines
Reconciling key accounts during the month, not only at the end
Automating repeat entries and reviewing the biggest risks first

questions.text: As an auditor, how would you test whether a client's recorded sales really happened?
covers: Picking a sample from recorded sales and tracing it to orders, delivery proof and receipts
Checking sales around the year end were recorded in the right period
Looking for unusual patterns, such as large credit notes just after the year end

questions.text: Which accounting software and Excel functions have you used, and for what?
covers: The packages you've used and the tasks you did in them
Excel: lookups, pivot tables and reconciliation work
How you'd pick up a new system quickly

questions.text: Tell me about yourself, and where you are with any professional qualification.
covers: Your education and experience in two or three lines
Your qualification status, stated honestly
The kind of accounting work you want next

questions.text: Why accounting, and are you aiming for audit, tax or finance in a company?
covers: What you like about the work, shown by an example
The path you prefer and why
How this job fits that path

questions.text: Year-end and audit season can mean long days. How do you handle that kind of pressure?
covers: An honest answer about your availability
An example of a busy period you managed well
How you keep accuracy up when you're tired

tips: Revise the everyday basics: journal entries, depreciation methods, reconciliations, accruals and prepayments.
Know the tax and compliance basics for the country of the job, and their filing cycles, at the level the role needs.
If you've done articleship or an internship, prepare two stories from it: an audit finding and something you improved.
Some roles include a practical test; practise pivot tables, lookups and a quick reconciliation in Excel.
When you're unsure of a rule, say how you'd check it, such as the standard or a senior, rather than guessing.
Be exact about your qualification status and dates; interviewers commonly ask.
